A plant turns toward the sun, but it doesn't feel the sun the way you feel warmth on your face. It has no brain and no nerves, which are the parts of the body that let us feel pain. A little pig has them. And there's more: to raise a little pig, you have to give him lots of plants to eat. So people who eat plants directly end up using far fewer plants than people who eat animals.

Plants react to their environment, but there's no evidence they feel: they have no neurons, no brain, and nothing that plays their role. And even if they did feel, eating animals would be worse for plants, because animals eat a lot of plants before they become food: about a third of the calories grown by the world's crops go to animal feed. If plants matter, the conclusion is to eat plants.
"If plants did feel, wouldn't it be better to eat the plants than to eat those who eat lots of plants?"

A response to a stimulus, without anyone feeling it
A thermostat switches on the air conditioning; a plant turns toward the light
There being something it is like, for someone, to be in that state
Sentience is the capacity to have good or bad experiences. It requires some structure capable of integrating information into an experience, and in animals that's linked to the nervous system.

text.bold: 1. There's no evidence of experience in plants.

paragraph.text: In 2019, a group of plant biologists published a review concluding that plants neither possess nor require consciousness: they have no neurons or brain, and there's no evolutionary reason for them to have developed costly mental faculties. The same authors don't deny that plants have complex behavior, which is another matter.

Plants react to touch, light and damage, as many mindless systems do. The word "communication", used for chemical signals between plants, is a metaphor: it doesn't imply that anyone is listening or suffering.

text.bold: 3. Intelligence isn't consciousness, however counterintuitive that sounds.

paragraph.text: Solving problems, learning, adapting and making decisions are ways of processing information, and none of that requires anyone to be living the experience from the inside. The examples are close at hand: an artificial intelligence system writes, translates and plays chess better than most people, and as far as anyone knows feels nothing while doing it; a bacterium detects substances in its surroundings, computes a direction and swims toward food, and nobody credits it with an inner experience. Plants belong in that category: they do remarkable things, some of them resembling memory and learning, with no evidence that there is anything it is like to be a plant. What sentience asks for isn't performance, it's a point of view. And the reverse holds too: a simple mind that solves no problems at all can suffer a great deal.

text.bold: 4. Even if they felt, eating animals would be worse.

paragraph.text: Animals have to eat plants to grow. About 36% of the calories from the world's crops go to animal feed, and only about 12% of those calories reach people as meat, milk and eggs. Eating plants directly uses far fewer plants.
If plants' possible capacity to feel cancelled every moral difference, there'd be no difference between eating a lettuce and eating a dog, or a human. Almost no one accepts that.

text.bold: 6. The doubt tends to be selective.

paragraph.text: Concern for plants almost always comes up as a reply to veganism, not as a reason to change how one treats them. That doesn't refute the argument, but it suggests it isn't the real reason of those who use it.

text.bold: 7. If plants mattered, eating animals would be the worst of both worlds.

paragraph.text: Animals raised for consumption eat far more plants than people would eat directly. Whoever takes seriously the idea that plants count should, for consistency, eat fewer animals, not more. Taken to the end, the conclusion would be fruitarianism, not a barbecue.

paragraph.text: (d) The strongest counter-reply: we don't know where consciousness begins

The most serious version doesn't say plants feel. It says we don't know where consciousness ends, that there are theories, such as some versions of panpsychism, that attribute some degree of experience to very simple systems, and that out of humility we shouldn't draw boundaries so confidently.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion
Admitting uncertainty isn't treating all hypotheses as equally likely. The evidence of sentience in vertebrates is strong; in plants, practically nil.

Plants are fascinating organisms, with responses to their environment more sophisticated than was once thought, and research on them deserves attention. It's also true that the science of consciousness has real uncertainties, and that humility is a good attitude toward them.

But the available evidence points in a clear direction: those with a nervous system can feel, and those without one very probably can't. And even if plants did feel, the conclusion wouldn't change: the way to cause them less harm would be to eat plants, not animals fed on them.
